claims.text: The precursor powders are nanocrystalline BCC solid solutions prepared by mechanical alloying.
Sintering at 1000 °C promotes formation of a more robust passive oxide film than sintering at 850–950 °C.
The high-temperature film is continuous, dense, spinel-type, and enriched in Al and Fe.
High-temperature sintering causes surface elemental enrichment before protective oxide formation.
The oxide film limits diffusion of corrosive species into the alloy.
The oxide film has sufficiently high hardness to resist mechanical removal.
The protective film reduces the effective active surface area available for corrosion.
The protective film minimizes material loss from wear.
The film's combined diffusion-barrier and wear-resistance functions reduce degradation during simultaneous corrosion and mechanical wear.
Alloys sintered at 850–950 °C form a less robust passive film than the alloy sintered at 1000 °C.
The lower-temperature alloys exhibit a predominant direct-attack corrosion mode.
The lower-temperature alloys have inferior wear resistance.
The 1000 °C alloy has a lower corrosion current density than the alloys sintered at 850–950 °C.
The 1000 °C alloy has higher charge-transfer or passive-film resistance than the lower-temperature alloys.
The 1000 °C alloy will have a lower wear-scar volume than the lower-temperature alloys.
Under simultaneous wear and corrosion, degradation of the 1000 °C alloy will be reduced relative to the summed individual degradation effects in the baseline.
The prediction should hold when oxygen is available to support oxide-film formation.
The prediction should hold under moderate abrasive conditions.
The prediction may fail under extremely abrasive conditions because the film can be removed faster than it protects the substrate.
The prediction may fail under oxygen-starved conditions because oxide-film formation is suppressed.
